passage: By the time the sun climbed over the wheat, Kamal had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework. His mother Rukmini watched him from the doorway, holding her tea. "You're up early. Again." "Just helping, Ma." He kept sweeping. All week he had been doing this. Under it sat a small hard thought: if he hadn't argued so much with his brother, if he had scored better in maths, maybe his parents wouldn't be splitting up. Rukmini set down her tea and sat on the step. "Kamal, come here. Your father and I have talked. Nothing you did caused this. Nothing." His broom slowed. His shoulders shook. "You can love us both, and you don't have to be perfect for us."

qa.q: What had Kamal finished before sunrise?
qa.a: He had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework.

qa.q: What secret thought was Kamal carrying under all his chores?
qa.a: He wondered whether his arguments with his brother or his maths marks had caused his parents' split, which made him try to be perfect.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do that helped Kamal, and what could he do next?
qa.a: She told him plainly that nothing he did caused it. He can keep loving both parents and let the chores go back to normal, instead of trying to fix them by behaving perfectly.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel seeing her son work so hard all week?
qa.a: Probably worried and sad, since the extra chores told her Kamal was carrying something heavy, and she chose to answer it with plain, clear words.

grounding: Shows a teen secretly wondering if his fights or grades caused his parents' split, trying to be perfect, and hearing plainly that it was not his fault.
